findings.evidence: Three div.step elements in DOM order: s3-step3 (Confirm your order), s3-step2 (Enter payment details), s3-step1 (Choose a plan). CSS order property reverses visual display to 1, 2, 3 but screen reader linearizes as 3, 2, 1.
findings.violation: DOM reading order is reversed from the logical task sequence. A screen reader user hears steps as Confirm, then Enter payment, then Choose plan, when the correct sequence is Choose, Enter payment, Confirm. This reversal breaks task comprehension.
findings.fix: Reorder the DOM to match logical sequence: move s3-step1 before s3-step2, and s3-step2 before s3-step3, then remove or adjust CSS order properties to match.

findings.evidence: Label element with id s3-form-phone-label carries inline style color:#cc0000 (red). No asterisk, no required attribute, no aria-required, no other textual indicator.
findings.violation: The phone field label is colored red while all other form labels remain black. If the red color signals required status, color is the only way to distinguish this field from optional fields. A color-blind user cannot tell which fields are required.
findings.fix: Add a visual indicator beyond color: an asterisk after the label text, or add required attribute to the input and restyle to not rely on color alone.

findings.evidence: Promo input carries aria-invalid=true. Error text reads: Error.
findings.violation: The error message is generic and does not identify what is wrong with the promo code or how to correct it. A user cannot determine why the field was rejected or what format is expected.
findings.fix: Replace 'Error.' with specific guidance such as 'Promo code must be 6-8 alphanumeric characters' or 'Promo code not found in our system. Consult the field's required format.'
